name: Professional microneedling / RF microneedling

lead: Professional microneedling uses a device with many fine needles to make controlled punctures in the skin; RF microneedling adds radiofrequency energy through the needles. Clinics offer it for acne scars, fine lines, skin laxity, enlarged pores and texture, with the payoff of smoother skin and softer scars.

The needles create small channels and a wound-healing response described as stimulating collagen and elastin production, and RF versions heat the dermis around the needle tips. Trials have tested it for acne scars, melasma, skin laxity and hair loss, and combined with platelet-rich plasma or exosomes. Systematic reviews report it as efficacious in melasma but not clearly better than topical hydroquinone, and a review found evidence for adding PRP to microneedling for acne scars less supportive than for PRP with fractional laser.

paras: Done in a dermatology or aesthetic clinic, usually as a series of sessions, with serums or PRP sometimes applied during treatment. On looksmaxxing forums it is often compared with at-home dermarolling, and some users recommend clinic RF treatment over deeper home needling. Redness settles over a few days.

Reported effects include redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding, with infection and scarring possible. In 2024 the US CDC reported HIV infections linked to a spa offering PRP microneedling facials, prompting warnings about non-clinical settings. Devices and sterile technique matter, and licensed clinicians should perform it.

angle.text: Needles trigger the skin's healing response so new collagen forms, smoothing texture and softening scars over weeks. Trials support scar and texture use; claims about denser beard, eyebrow or scalp hair have been studied less.

lead: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy or skin needling, is a cosmetic procedure in which fine needles repeatedly puncture the skin to trigger a healing response. Professional versions use motorized pens with adjustable needle depth, and radiofrequency (RF) microneedling adds energy delivered through the needles to heat the deeper skin. [1]

Reviews list applications including acne scars, rhytides, surgical scars, pigment disorders, enlarged pores, stretch marks and transdermal delivery of topical drugs, and describe the technique as minimally invasive. [2][3][4] Trials have tested it for acne scars, melasma, skin laxity, hair loss and combined with platelet-rich plasma or exosomes.

The evidence is mixed by indication: systematic reviews report microneedling as efficacious in melasma but not clearly better than the standard topical hydroquinone, and a review found evidence for adding PRP to microneedling for acne scars less supportive than for PRP with fractional laser.  On looksmax.org, users discuss at-home dermarolling at length, while some recommend dermatology-office RF microneedling for deeper work. [5]
infobox: Needle pen/roller microneedling; fractional RF microneedling
Acne scars, texture, fine lines, laxity, some pigment and hair uses

paras: Microneedling devices include rollers, stamps and automated pens. Reviews describe a long period of innovation in the instruments since the technique was introduced for skin rejuvenation. [2][6] A 2009 paper described microneedling with the dermaroller as an approach to collagen induction. [7]
RF microneedling combines mechanical needling with radiofrequency energy. A 2021 review published in Dermatologic Surgery gave a comprehensive and critical overview of the technology.

Clinicians combine needling with topical or injected agents. PRP reviews describe pairing PRP with microneedling, lasers, fillers and fat grafting.  A 2019 review of PRP described its promise but called for standardized protocols.  Exosome solutions are an emerging additive, tested in a 12-week split-face trial and compared with PRP in a non-inferiority trial.

Acne scars: a randomized split-face study compared PRP with microneedling to microneedling with distilled water, and a 2023 randomized trial tested fractional microneedling RF combined with ablative fractional laser against laser alone for acne and acne scars. [8] A systematic review of PRP for acne scars found support for PRP with fractional ablative laser and less supportive evidence for PRP with microneedling.

Skin laxity and aging: a 2024 randomized trial found that microneedling RF enhanced penetration of poly-L-lactic acid and improved facial skin laxity; another randomized trial combined adipose-derived exosomes with microneedling for facial aging.  A non-inferiority trial compared exosomes with PRP in photoaged skin.

Melasma: a systematic review reported that microneedling and peeling were efficacious but that their superiority to topical hydroquinone remains unestablished, with high recurrence across all treatments; a randomized study compared tranexamic acid microinjections with and without microneedling. [9]

Hair: a randomized evaluator-blinded pilot study examined microneedling in androgenetic alopecia, and a randomized placebo-controlled study tested microneedling plus topical dutasteride; a systematic review of alopecia management lists procedural options including PRP among those reporting hair growth. [10]
Registered trials include RF microneedling studies in hypertrophic scars, photoaging, laxity and cellulite, several completed with small samples. [11][12][13]

Reviews describe the procedure as simple and safe when performed correctly. [2] Reports indicate that microneedling combined with blood-derived products in non-medical settings raised infection-control concerns. In April 2024 the CDC reported HIV diagnoses in three women who had received PRP microneedling facials at a New Mexico spa, and the New Mexico Department of Health had earlier warned of blood-borne infection risk from such treatments. [14]

Forum posts and guides about microneedling are common on looksmax.org, including at-home dermaroller and stamp guides aimed at acne scarring, beard and eyebrow growth, and threads about combining it with topicals such as tretinoin or peptides.  One user in a home-needling thread acknowledged that rollers reach only superficial scarring and that longer needles are riskier at home.

Opinions differ. Some users advise running deeper needling only infrequently and recommend dermatologist RF microneedling instead of deeper home use. [5] Another thread quotes a view that collagen made as a stress response is unhealthy, and users argue over this.

lore.intro: Microneedling is a staple of looksmax.org skin and facial hair discussion, with threads on home dermarolling guides and on clinic RF treatment. [5]
